title: AI reshapes global labour market into two distinct paths, rewarding human skills: PwC 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer
key_claim: The average AI-skills wage premium rose to 62% in 2026 (up from 57%), ranging from as high as 118% in consumer markets to 16% in government, while jobs demanding AI skills grew nearly eight times faster than the wider market, across more than one billion job advertisements in 27 countries.
frame_summary: AI is splitting the labour market into two tracks and rewarding AI-plus-human skills with a large, widening within-role pay premium.
verbatim_quote: As companies continue to boost productivity with AI, the average wage premium for workers with AI skills continued to surge higher – hitting 62%, up from 57% last year.
notes: Spine source, live-verified via WebFetch. 62% and 57% carried in verbatim_quote; 118% / 16% sector spread carried in key_claim.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Entry-Level Work: A Framework for Safeguarding and Reinventing Early Career Pathways
key_claim: More than one in three young workers are in occupations with medium-to-high exposure to AI-driven task change, so AI is changing the tasks and skills demanded within roles rather than simply removing jobs.
frame_summary: AI is reshaping how organisations hire, develop and advance talent within roles, most visibly at entry level, requiring deliberate action to safeguard early-career pathways.
verbatim_quote: Globally, more than one in three young workers are employed in occupations with medium to high exposure to AI-driven task change.
notes: Tier 2 institutional source on within-role task change, live-verified via WebFetch.

title: Navigating Skills Trends: Data Dashboard Analysis, April 2026 (Lightcast AI Skills Dashboard)
key_claim: US job postings requiring AI skills grew about 144% year over year as of April 2026, against roughly 7% growth for overall postings, so AI-skill demand more than doubled while general hiring was near flat.
frame_summary: Employer demand for AI skills is strong, fast-growing, geographically pervasive and spreading beyond the tech sector.
verbatim_quote: As of May 2026, the number of job postings in the United States that include AI skills had more than doubled compared to one year prior.
notes: Analysis of Lightcast AI Skills Dashboard data. 144% / 7% carried in key_claim; body uses the doubling framing. Live-verified via WebFetch.

title: AI and skills: What we know so far
key_claim: OECD research finds that skills, not job titles, determine who benefits from AI: AI shifts demand toward higher-level and human skills and is associated with posted wage premiums, while skill shortages constrain adoption.
frame_summary: Skills determine who captures AI's gains, so building AI and complementary human skills across the workforce is the priority.
verbatim_quote: This policy brief summarises and brings together various pieces of OECD research to build a coherent narrative on what we know about artificial intelligence (AI) and skills.
notes: Tier 1 (OECD) synthesis supporting the skills-over-titles framing. Live-verified via WebFetch; PDF body not machine-fetchable so verbatim is the on-page abstract.

title: Entry-level work didn't disappear, PwC finds with 'seniorization.' It just morphed into something young workers can't get
date_evidence: By Nick Lichtenberg — June 18, 2026, 12:45 PM ET
key_claim: Reporting on PwC's Barometer, Fortune finds that in the most AI-exposed occupations 52% of new skills appearing in entry-level postings are ones traditionally tied to experienced workers, so identical titles now demand senior-level capability.
frame_summary: AI is not erasing jobs so much as quietly reorganising who can do them; the same title now sorts workers by whether they bring AI-plus-judgment skills.
verbatim_quote: In the most AI-exposed occupations, 52% of new skills appearing in entry-level job postings were skills traditionally associated with experienced workers.
notes: Tier 3 quality journalism, live-verified via WebFetch. Carries the 52% within-title skill-shift figure.

title: Does Generative AI Narrow Education-Based Productivity Gaps? Evidence from a Randomized Experiment (Working Paper 34851)
key_claim: In a randomized experiment, generative AI raised productivity for everyone but helped lower-education workers most, cutting the education-based performance gap from 0.548 to 0.139 standard deviations, so AI compressed rather than widened within-task skill gaps.
frame_summary: Counter-evidence: generative AI acts as a leveller, disproportionately lifting lower-skilled workers and compressing intra-group productivity, and by implication pay, gaps.
verbatim_quote: AI increases productivity for all participants, with substantially larger gains for lower-education individuals.
notes: Counter-argument source (Tier 1 primary randomized experiment). Live-verified via WebFetch; the 0.548-to-0.139 SD figure is analyst-cited from the abstract.

title: Payscale's 2026 Compensation Best Practices Report Reveals Shifting Pay Strategies Amid AI and Labor Market Volatility
key_claim: 61% of organisations have rewritten existing roles to require AI-related skills or competencies, yet 55% are not adjusting compensation for those skills, so employers are re-architecting job requirements around AI faster than they re-price them.
frame_summary: Employers are rapidly rebuilding job requirements around AI proficiency while formal pay differentiation for AI skills still lags, so the premium is real in the market but only partly written into pay structures.
verbatim_quote: Sixty-one percent of orgs have updated existing roles to include AI-related skills or competencies, but 55% are not adjusting compensation for those skills.
notes: Structural anchor, 144 days before scan date (within 6 months): canonical comp-practices data on employers re-writing roles faster than pay. Live-verified via WebFetch; body spells out percentages as words.
